claims.assertion: The GPS track shows one off-route segment (17:41–17:44) in which the driver covered 1.76 km where the optimal route covers 0.03 km, adding 1.73 km and straying up to 979 m from the optimal route; under RD-1 that unexplained deviation is a route deviation and the driver bore the duty to take the shortest and most direct route.

The trip is a metered RydeTAXI trip, so the extra 1.73 km entered the meter and produced the billed excess of $2.90 (2.1 km × $1.41/km) — the refund figure is computed from the fare's own per-km rate applied to the unexcused segment's extra_km, i.e. 1.73 km × $1.41 = $2.44.

No chat record shows the driver proposing a route change before leaving the optimal route, or any rider agreement to it: the only messages are the rider's 17:24 pickup note and the driver's 17:24 arrival note, both before the 17:41 deviation.

The driver's written excuse ("accident on Seletar Expressway, lanes blocked") does not exempt the segment: the only congestion corroboration on the optimal route is speed band 4 (30–39 km/h), not band 1 or 2, and a single band record cannot exempt a segment on its own.

The reported accident 0 m from the optimal route was logged at 17:16, before the 17:41 deviation, but it sits on the Seletar Expressway while the deviation carried the car up to 979 m off the optimal route onto a 1.76 km detour — the traffic record therefore does not cover the alternative the driver actually took, and the detour's extra_km remains unexcused.

No published surcharge applies to this trip: waiting fee is $0.00, no surge (1.0×), and the billed $40.18 consists only of base $3.90, distance $27.23, time $7.58 and platform $1.47, so the meter excess is confined to the off-route distance refunded under C2.

The driver's 90-day record shows 1 upheld dispute already, so if the panel finds this deviation upheld, this case makes the conduct repeated and warrants an account review referral alongside the refund.

weaknesses: The driver has a documented traffic justification (F12: accident logged at 17:16, 0 m from the optimal route, lanes blocked) plus a matching congestion band on the optimal route (F10, band 4), so the panel may treat RD-4 as satisfied in substance and exempt the segment even though the band is not 1 or 2.

The measured deviation is small in relative terms — +2.1 km / +12% overall (F1) and a 1.76 km segment (F3) — so a panel could call it a minor or map-matching artifact rather than a material route breach.

My client is not a clean complainant: 2 disputes in 90 days with 0 upheld (F14), and there is no rider-side evidence of a request for the direct route beyond the absence of agreement (F7, F8), which the driver's side may use to argue the rider was indifferent.

The refund I can claim is limited to the meter excess; because the ride was metered RydeTAXI with $0.00 waiting (F6), I cannot claim the wait/stops component or any unpublished fee, and the $2.44 figure derives from the fare's per-km rate rather than any Ryde-published formula.

claims.assertion: The single off-route segment (17:41–17:44, 1.76 km driven where the optimal route covers 0.03 km, adding 1.73 km) coincides with a logged accident on the optimal route: an Accident/Lanes-blocked incident was reported at 17:16 directly on the optimal route (0 m from it), which is before the segment started and which falls inside the 17:18–18:02 window covering the trip, so this segment is exempt under RD-4(a).

The reroute decision was corroborated by recorded congestion on the alternative and no weather excuse: the optimal-route corridor shows speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) on the Seletar Expressway during 17:18–18:02 and band 5 on the Tampines Expressway over the same window, with fair weather (0.0 mm rain).

There is no passenger-agreement defect to weigh against the driver: the chat log contains only two pickup-coordination messages (rider 17:24 at main entrance, driver 17:24 arriving in 2 min), so no route change was discussed with or requested by the rider, and the driver's claim rests entirely on the traffic record rather than on chat.

Because the only off-route segment is exempt under RD-4(a), the remaining distance gap is at most 0.37 km (2.1 km total excess minus the 1.73 km exempt segment), which is within the 0.25 km map-matching residual plus rounding scale contemplated by RD-2 and not attributable to any unexplained violation.

The bill itself contains no unannounced add-on: the total of $40.18 is comprised of base $3.90, metered distance $27.23 (19.3 km), metered time $7.58 (29.2 min), waiting $0.00 and platform fee $1.47, at a 1.0× multiplier, so no unpublished item was added to the fare.

Any mileage refund on the RydeTAXI meter is limited to the unexempt segments' extra km at the trip's per-km rate; here the exempt segment's 1.73 km falls away, so the amount computable from the fare facts is at most $0.52 (0.37 km × $1.41/km) and, on the exemption analysis, $0.00.

Flagging this driver's account would be unwarranted: the driver has 6.0 years on the platform, a 4.76 rating, 831 trips in 90 days, and his only upheld dispute in 90 days was not a route case, so the 'repeated route deviation' condition is not met.

weaknesses: The excess is real on the meter: actual 19.3 km vs optimal 17.3 km (+2.1 km, +12%) and 29.2 min vs 24 min (F1, F2), and the rider will argue the whole 2.1 km should be refunded at $1.41/km, i.e. the $2.90 excess billed (F4, F6) — the driver conceded no consent in chat (F7, F8).

The exempt segment only accounts for 1.73 km of the 2.1 km excess (F1, F3); the rider can point to the residual ~0.37 km as unexplained mileage, and RD-2 only excuses up to a 0.25 km matching residual, so part of the gap (F4) may not be covered.

The traffic defence rests on congestion and one incident: the band data available is only band 4/5 (30–39 / 40–49 km/h) (F10, F11), which is not band 1–2, so band evidence alone cannot carry the exemption (RD-4(b)); if the judge reads the 17:16 accident as cleared too early, the segment reverts to RD-2 (F12).

The driver never messaged the rider about the reroute — the only chat is pickup coordination (F7, F8) — so the rider's objection that no agreement existed is factually accurate, leaving the case resting solely on the traffic record (F12).

events.title: Rider Advocate rebuttal: 8 points
events.body:
→ D1: RD-4(a) requires the incident to correspond to the part of the optimal route that was replaced; the accident was logged on the Seletar Expressway at 0 m from the optimal route (F12), whereas the driver's deviation took the car up to 979 m off the optimal route over a 1.76 km detour (F3), so the cited incident does not cover the alternative actually driven and the segment stays unexcused. [F12 F3] [RD-4]
→ D2: The driver's own congestion evidence fails his own clause: the recorded bands are 4 and 5 (30–39 and 40–49 km/h) on the Seletar and Tampines Expressways (F10, F11), not band 1 or 2, and RD-4(b) says band data cannot exempt a segment on its own, so this corroboration cannot carry the exemption. [F10 F11 F13] [RD-4]
→ D3: The absence of any chat about a route change cuts against the driver, not for him: under RD-5 the driver had to reach agreement before leaving the optimal route, and the only messages are 17:24 pickup coordination (F7, F8) — the deviation began at 17:41 (F3). [F7 F8 F3] [RD-5]
→ D4: The residual-gap argument is moot here: there is only one off-route segment of 1.73 km (F3), and once it is not exempt under RD-4 the whole of it is the refund base, leaving no residual to characterise; the 0.25 km residual remark in RD-2 is a data-layer parameter, not a clause. [F1 F3] [RD-2 RD-1]
→ D5 (concedes): Concede that the bill lists no unpublished add-on — waiting is $0.00, surge is 1.0× and the components are base, distance, time and platform only (F5, F6) — but the refund sought is exactly the metered distance excess produced by the unexempt segment, not a new fee. [F4 F5 F6] [FARE-1 RD-2]
→ D6: The $0.52 alternative cannot be reached because it depends on the same failed exemption: with the 1.73 km segment unexempt, RD-2 gives the refund as extra_km × the trip's per-km rate, i.e. 1.73 km × $1.41 = $2.44 (F3, F4). [F3 F4] [RD-2 RD-4]
→ D7: RD-6's account-review trigger is a repeated-or-severe concern, and the driver's own record shows 1 upheld dispute in 90 days (F15); the flag is an ancillary referral request only, not the basis of the route finding, which rests on F3 and F12. [F15 F3] [RD-6]
→ C7 (concedes): Withdraw the account-review referral as a practical matter: the rider's case does not depend on it, and it is not needed for the refund under C2. [F15] [RD-6]

points.response: RD-4(a) requires the incident to correspond to the part of the optimal route that was replaced; the accident was logged on the Seletar Expressway at 0 m from the optimal route (F12), whereas the driver's deviation took the car up to 979 m off the optimal route over a 1.76 km detour (F3), so the cited incident does not cover the alternative actually driven and the segment stays unexcused.

The driver's own congestion evidence fails his own clause: the recorded bands are 4 and 5 (30–39 and 40–49 km/h) on the Seletar and Tampines Expressways (F10, F11), not band 1 or 2, and RD-4(b) says band data cannot exempt a segment on its own, so this corroboration cannot carry the exemption.

The absence of any chat about a route change cuts against the driver, not for him: under RD-5 the driver had to reach agreement before leaving the optimal route, and the only messages are 17:24 pickup coordination (F7, F8) — the deviation began at 17:41 (F3).

The residual-gap argument is moot here: there is only one off-route segment of 1.73 km (F3), and once it is not exempt under RD-4 the whole of it is the refund base, leaving no residual to characterise; the 0.25 km residual remark in RD-2 is a data-layer parameter, not a clause.

Concede that the bill lists no unpublished add-on — waiting is $0.00, surge is 1.0× and the components are base, distance, time and platform only (F5, F6) — but the refund sought is exactly the metered distance excess produced by the unexempt segment, not a new fee.

The $0.52 alternative cannot be reached because it depends on the same failed exemption: with the 1.73 km segment unexempt, RD-2 gives the refund as extra_km × the trip's per-km rate, i.e. 1.73 km × $1.41 = $2.44 (F3, F4).

RD-6's account-review trigger is a repeated-or-severe concern, and the driver's own record shows 1 upheld dispute in 90 days (F15); the flag is an ancillary referral request only, not the basis of the route finding, which rests on F3 and F12.
Withdraw the account-review referral as a practical matter: the rider's case does not depend on it, and it is not needed for the refund under C2.

events.body:
→ C1 (concedes): Conceded in part: an off-route segment does exist (F3), but RD-1 liability is not self-executing — each segment must be run through RD-3/RD-4/RD-5, and this one is answered by the RD-4(a) traffic record (F12), so the segment is not an 'unexempted' segment. [F3 F12] [RD-1 RD-4]
→ C2: The $2.44 figure assumes the whole 1.73 km extra_km is unexempted, which RD-4(a) defeats (F3, F12); because the segment is exempt, the refund-computable amount under RD-2 is $0.00, not $2.44. [F3 F12 F4] [RD-2 RD-4]
→ C3: C3 is true but irrelevant to my defence: I do not rely on rider consent under RD-5, I rely on the RD-4(a) 'reasonable cause' exception, which needs no chat agreement — the only messages are pickup coordination at 17:24 (F7, F8). [F7 F8] [RD-5 RD-4]

[F12 F10 F11] [RD-4]
→ C5: C5 misreads RD-4(a): the clause requires the incident to sit on the substituted (optimal) section, which the record does at 0 m from the optimal route (F12); that 17:16 blockage is precisely why a 1.76 km detour carrying the car up to 979 m off the optimal route was taken (F3), and the resulting duration of 29.2 min vs 24 min (F2) is consistent with an incident-related diversion rather than an unexplained joyride. [F12 F3 F2] [RD-4]

→ C7: C7 fails RD-6's own condition: the driver's single upheld 90-day dispute was not a route case, so this is not a 'repeated' route deviation, and the rider's own record shows 2 disputes with 0 upheld (F14, F15). [F15 F14] [RD-6]

The $2.44 figure assumes the whole 1.73 km extra_km is unexempted, which RD-4(a) defeats (F3, F12); because the segment is exempt, the refund-computable amount under RD-2 is $0.00, not $2.44.

C3 is true but irrelevant to my defence: I do not rely on rider consent under RD-5, I rely on the RD-4(a) 'reasonable cause' exception, which needs no chat agreement — the only messages are pickup coordination at 17:24 (F7, F8).

C4 attacks the band corroboration only: RD-4(a) is independently satisfied by the LTA incident itself — an Accident/Lanes-blocked event reported 17:16 at 0 m from the optimal route, before the 17:41 segment and inside a window still listing the condition at 17:18–18:02 — with bands band 4 (F10) and band 5 (F11) serving as the (b) corroboration, not as the sole basis.

C5 misreads RD-4(a): the clause requires the incident to sit on the substituted (optimal) section, which the record does at 0 m from the optimal route (F12); that 17:16 blockage is precisely why a 1.76 km detour carrying the car up to 979 m off the optimal route was taken (F3), and the resulting duration of 29.2 min vs 24 min (F2) is consistent with an incident-related diversion rather than an unexplained joyride.

claims.assertion: The GPS track shows one off-route segment (17:41–17:44) in which the driver covered 1.76 km where the optimal route covers 0.03 km, adding 1.73 km and straying up to 979 m from the optimal route; under RD-1 that unexplained deviation is a route deviation and the driver bore the duty to take the shortest and most direct route.

The trip is a metered RydeTAXI trip, so the extra 1.73 km entered the meter and produced the billed excess of $2.90 (2.1 km × $1.41/km) — the refund figure is computed from the fare's own per-km rate applied to the unexcused segment's extra_km, i.e. 1.73 km × $1.41 = $2.44.

No chat record shows the driver proposing a route change before leaving the optimal route, or any rider agreement to it: the only messages are the rider's 17:24 pickup note and the driver's 17:24 arrival note, both before the 17:41 deviation.

The driver's written excuse ("accident on Seletar Expressway, lanes blocked") does not exempt the segment: the only congestion corroboration on the optimal route is speed band 4 (30–39 km/h), not band 1 or 2, and a single band record cannot exempt a segment on its own.

The reported accident 0 m from the optimal route was logged at 17:16, before the 17:41 deviation, but it sits on the Seletar Expressway while the deviation carried the car up to 979 m off the optimal route onto a 1.76 km detour — the traffic record therefore does not cover the alternative the driver actually took, and the detour's extra_km remains unexcused.

No published surcharge applies to this trip: waiting fee is $0.00, no surge (1.0×), and the billed $40.18 consists only of base $3.90, distance $27.23, time $7.58 and platform $1.47, so the meter excess is confined to the off-route distance refunded under C2.

The driver's 90-day record shows 1 upheld dispute already, so if the panel finds this deviation upheld, this case makes the conduct repeated and warrants an account review referral alongside the refund.

weaknesses: The driver has a documented traffic justification (F12: accident logged at 17:16, 0 m from the optimal route, lanes blocked) plus a matching congestion band on the optimal route (F10, band 4), so the panel may treat RD-4 as satisfied in substance and exempt the segment even though the band is not 1 or 2.

The measured deviation is small in relative terms — +2.1 km / +12% overall (F1) and a 1.76 km segment (F3) — so a panel could call it a minor or map-matching artifact rather than a material route breach.

My client is not a clean complainant: 2 disputes in 90 days with 0 upheld (F14), and there is no rider-side evidence of a request for the direct route beyond the absence of agreement (F7, F8), which the driver's side may use to argue the rider was indifferent.

The refund I can claim is limited to the meter excess; because the ride was metered RydeTAXI with $0.00 waiting (F6), I cannot claim the wait/stops component or any unpublished fee, and the $2.44 figure derives from the fare's per-km rate rather than any Ryde-published formula.

claims.assertion: The single off-route segment (17:41–17:44, 1.76 km driven where the optimal route covers 0.03 km, adding 1.73 km) coincides with a logged accident on the optimal route: an Accident/Lanes-blocked incident was reported at 17:16 directly on the optimal route (0 m from it), which is before the segment started and which falls inside the 17:18–18:02 window covering the trip, so this segment is exempt under RD-4(a).

The reroute decision was corroborated by recorded congestion on the alternative and no weather excuse: the optimal-route corridor shows speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) on the Seletar Expressway during 17:18–18:02 and band 5 on the Tampines Expressway over the same window, with fair weather (0.0 mm rain).

There is no passenger-agreement defect to weigh against the driver: the chat log contains only two pickup-coordination messages (rider 17:24 at main entrance, driver 17:24 arriving in 2 min), so no route change was discussed with or requested by the rider, and the driver's claim rests entirely on the traffic record rather than on chat.

Because the only off-route segment is exempt under RD-4(a), the remaining distance gap is at most 0.37 km (2.1 km total excess minus the 1.73 km exempt segment), which is within the 0.25 km map-matching residual plus rounding scale contemplated by RD-2 and not attributable to any unexplained violation.

The bill itself contains no unannounced add-on: the total of $40.18 is comprised of base $3.90, metered distance $27.23 (19.3 km), metered time $7.58 (29.2 min), waiting $0.00 and platform fee $1.47, at a 1.0× multiplier, so no unpublished item was added to the fare.

Any mileage refund on the RydeTAXI meter is limited to the unexempt segments' extra km at the trip's per-km rate; here the exempt segment's 1.73 km falls away, so the amount computable from the fare facts is at most $0.52 (0.37 km × $1.41/km) and, on the exemption analysis, $0.00.

Flagging this driver's account would be unwarranted: the driver has 6.0 years on the platform, a 4.76 rating, 831 trips in 90 days, and his only upheld dispute in 90 days was not a route case, so the 'repeated route deviation' condition is not met.

weaknesses: The excess is real on the meter: actual 19.3 km vs optimal 17.3 km (+2.1 km, +12%) and 29.2 min vs 24 min (F1, F2), and the rider will argue the whole 2.1 km should be refunded at $1.41/km, i.e. the $2.90 excess billed (F4, F6) — the driver conceded no consent in chat (F7, F8).

The exempt segment only accounts for 1.73 km of the 2.1 km excess (F1, F3); the rider can point to the residual ~0.37 km as unexplained mileage, and RD-2 only excuses up to a 0.25 km matching residual, so part of the gap (F4) may not be covered.

The traffic defence rests on congestion and one incident: the band data available is only band 4/5 (30–39 / 40–49 km/h) (F10, F11), which is not band 1–2, so band evidence alone cannot carry the exemption (RD-4(b)); if the judge reads the 17:16 accident as cleared too early, the segment reverts to RD-2 (F12).

The driver never messaged the rider about the reroute — the only chat is pickup coordination (F7, F8) — so the rider's objection that no agreement existed is factually accurate, leaving the case resting solely on the traffic record (F12).

points.response: RD-4(a) requires the incident to correspond to the part of the optimal route that was replaced; the accident was logged on the Seletar Expressway at 0 m from the optimal route (F12), whereas the driver's deviation took the car up to 979 m off the optimal route over a 1.76 km detour (F3), so the cited incident does not cover the alternative actually driven and the segment stays unexcused.

The driver's own congestion evidence fails his own clause: the recorded bands are 4 and 5 (30–39 and 40–49 km/h) on the Seletar and Tampines Expressways (F10, F11), not band 1 or 2, and RD-4(b) says band data cannot exempt a segment on its own, so this corroboration cannot carry the exemption.

The absence of any chat about a route change cuts against the driver, not for him: under RD-5 the driver had to reach agreement before leaving the optimal route, and the only messages are 17:24 pickup coordination (F7, F8) — the deviation began at 17:41 (F3).

The residual-gap argument is moot here: there is only one off-route segment of 1.73 km (F3), and once it is not exempt under RD-4 the whole of it is the refund base, leaving no residual to characterise; the 0.25 km residual remark in RD-2 is a data-layer parameter, not a clause.

Concede that the bill lists no unpublished add-on — waiting is $0.00, surge is 1.0× and the components are base, distance, time and platform only (F5, F6) — but the refund sought is exactly the metered distance excess produced by the unexempt segment, not a new fee.

The $0.52 alternative cannot be reached because it depends on the same failed exemption: with the 1.73 km segment unexempt, RD-2 gives the refund as extra_km × the trip's per-km rate, i.e. 1.73 km × $1.41 = $2.44 (F3, F4).

RD-6's account-review trigger is a repeated-or-severe concern, and the driver's own record shows 1 upheld dispute in 90 days (F15); the flag is an ancillary referral request only, not the basis of the route finding, which rests on F3 and F12.
Withdraw the account-review referral as a practical matter: the rider's case does not depend on it, and it is not needed for the refund under C2.

Conceded in part: an off-route segment does exist (F3), but RD-1 liability is not self-executing — each segment must be run through RD-3/RD-4/RD-5, and this one is answered by the RD-4(a) traffic record (F12), so the segment is not an 'unexempted' segment.
The $2.44 figure assumes the whole 1.73 km extra_km is unexempted, which RD-4(a) defeats (F3, F12); because the segment is exempt, the refund-computable amount under RD-2 is $0.00, not $2.44.

C3 is true but irrelevant to my defence: I do not rely on rider consent under RD-5, I rely on the RD-4(a) 'reasonable cause' exception, which needs no chat agreement — the only messages are pickup coordination at 17:24 (F7, F8).

C4 attacks the band corroboration only: RD-4(a) is independently satisfied by the LTA incident itself — an Accident/Lanes-blocked event reported 17:16 at 0 m from the optimal route, before the 17:41 segment and inside a window still listing the condition at 17:18–18:02 — with bands band 4 (F10) and band 5 (F11) serving as the (b) corroboration, not as the sole basis.

C5 misreads RD-4(a): the clause requires the incident to sit on the substituted (optimal) section, which the record does at 0 m from the optimal route (F12); that 17:16 blockage is precisely why a 1.76 km detour carrying the car up to 979 m off the optimal route was taken (F3), and the resulting duration of 29.2 min vs 24 min (F2) is consistent with an incident-related diversion rather than an unexplained joyride.

Agreed on the arithmetic of the bill (F5, F6), but C6's conclusion still depends on the segment being unexempted; with RD-4(a) applying to the only off-route segment, no component of the metered fare is refundable.

C7 fails RD-6's own condition: the driver's single upheld 90-day dispute was not a route case, so this is not a 'repeated' route deviation, and the rider's own record shows 2 disputes with 0 upheld (F14, F15).
